claim: NFPA 72 emergency voice communication intelligibility acceptance is defined as at least 90% of measurement locations within each acoustically distinguishable space achieving STI >= 0.45 (CIS >= 0.65) with an average STI >= 0.50 (CIS >= 0.70) when quantitative measurement is performed.
source_title: Voice Intelligibility in Mass Notification Systems
source_citation: NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, Annex D and Chapter 18 (voice intelligibility criteria), National Fire Protection Association
page_or_section: Annex D; Chapter 18 intelligibility criteria (as summarized)
supporting_excerpt: The voice intelligibility of an emergency communication system is considered acceptable if at least 90 percent of the measurement locations within each ADS have a measured STI of not less than 0.45 (0.65 CIS) and an average STI of not less than 0.50 (0.70 CIS).
airport_or_entity: US building code (adopted through state/local codes; applied at IAD and DCA)
denominator: measurement locations per acoustically distinguishable space
caveat: NFPA 72 does not compel quantitative measurement in every case; a listen test may be accepted by the AHJ. Adoption depends on the enforcing jurisdiction's code cycle.

claim: 28 CFR 35.160 requires a public entity to take appropriate steps to ensure that communications with individuals with disabilities are as effective as communications with others and to furnish appropriate auxiliary aids and services, giving primary consideration to the individual's requested aid.
supporting_excerpt: A public entity shall take appropriate steps to ensure that communications with applicants, participants, members of the public, and companions with disabilities are as effective as communications with others... A public entity shall furnish appropriate auxiliary aids and services... In determining what type of auxiliary aid and service is necessary, a public entity shall give primary consideration to the requests of individuals with disabilities.
airport_or_entity: MWAA (as public entity under Title II)
caveat: Applies to MWAA operations directly; airline operations on airport premises are additionally covered by 14 CFR Part 382.

claim: 14 CFR Part 382 (Air Carrier Access Act rule) requires carriers to make aircraft, facilities, and services accessible; passengers who need visual or hearing assistance must receive prompt access to the same trip information as other passengers at gate, ticket area, customer service desk, and on the aircraft; and post-December 2016 airline-installed automated airport kiosks at US airports with 10,000+ enplanements/year must be accessible until 25% of installed machines at each airport are accessible.
source_title: eCFR :: 14 CFR Part 382 -- Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability in Air Travel
page_or_section: 14 CFR Part 382, Subparts A-B; kiosk provisions at Subpart D
supporting_excerpt: Passengers with disabilities have the right to receive information about services and aircraft capabilities and limitations, and the right to receive information in an accessible format... An airline's primary website must be accessible if the airline uses an aircraft with more than 60 seats... airlines must ensure that automated kiosks they install after December 2016 at U.S. airports with 10,000 or more enplanements per year are an accessible model, until 25% of kiosks at each airport location are the accessible model.
airport_or_entity: US carriers operating at IAD and DCA
denominator: airline-installed kiosks at each airport location
caveat: MWAA cannot enforce Part 382 on carriers directly; it can only require compliance through Use and Lease and tenant technology standards.

claim: The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (P.L. 118-63, enacted May 16, 2024) did not raise the PFC cap; the maximum PFC level remains $4.50 per boarded passenger, unchanged since 2000-2001.
source_title: Lawmakers Reach Agreement on Final FAA Bill (AAAE US Contract Tower Association alert on FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024)
page_or_section: PFC-related sections of P.L. 118-63 as summarized
supporting_excerpt: In the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (P.L. 118-63), Congress did not raise the PFC cap - the final legislation retained $4.50... The maximum PFC level was increased to $4.50 in 2000, and has not been adjusted since. The airport industry included the proposed increase of the PFC level as one of the major initiatives for the FAA reauthorization, but those efforts did not succeed in the 2024 reauthorization legislation.
airport_or_entity: US commercial airports including MWAA (IAD and DCA)
caveat: P.L. 118-63 did include PFC application-streamlining provisions; the cap itself was not raised.

claim: The Dulles Main Terminal (Saarinen) was determined eligible for the National Register of Historic Places in March 1978; the Dulles Historic District includes the Main Terminal, ATCT, mobile lounges, runways, terminal area landscaping, and the Dulles Airport Access Highway.
source_title: Federal Aviation Administration Section 3 Progress Report (Advisory Council on Historic Preservation)
supporting_excerpt: Dulles International Airport (IAD) was determined eligible for the National Register under Criteria A and C in 1978... The distinctive Main Terminal, air traffic control tower (ATCT) and several supporting buildings were determined to meet National Register criteria as part of a Historic District along with the mobile lounges, runways, terminal area landscaping, and the Dulles Airport Access Highway.
caveat: Eligibility is not the same as listing; the terminal was determined eligible but has not been formally added to the National Register. Section 106 obligations attach to eligible properties.

claim: The Dulles Corridor Metrorail Project's Refined Locally Preferred Alternative was found to have an 'Adverse Effect' on the Dulles Airport Historic District through landscape displacement at Saarinen Circle, requiring Section 106 mitigation.
source_title: Dulles Corridor Metrorail Project Phase - FTA Finding of No Significant Impact / Section 106 documentation
supporting_excerpt: The Refined LPA was found to have an 'Adverse Effect' on the Dulles Airport Historic District by displacing recent landscaping along Saarinen Circle.
caveat: Adverse Effect findings do not prohibit projects; they trigger consultation, memoranda of agreement, and mitigation.

claim: AIP grants cannot be used for exclusive-use areas in terminals, revenue-producing areas of terminals, hangars, or non-aviation development; the AIP Handbook Order 5100.38D is the operative eligibility document.
source_title: FAA AIP Overview - What is AIP & What is Eligible
supporting_excerpt: In general, sponsors can get AIP funds for most airfield capital improvements or rehabilitation projects and in some specific situations, for terminals, hangars, and nonaviation development... AIP grants cannot be used on exclusive-use areas in terminals, revenue producing areas of terminals, hangars and non-aviation development.
caveat: Some public-use portions of terminals may be AIP-eligible; the airfield noise attenuation program has separate rules. Case-by-case eligibility should be confirmed with the FAA Regional Airports Office.

claim: The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 authorized 10 additional daily beyond-perimeter slot exemptions at DCA (5 nonstop round-trips); DOT awarded these in December 2024 to Alaska (SEA), American (SAN), Delta (SFO), Southwest (SAT), and United (LAS), with service starts staggered from February through March 2025. DCA slot control and the perimeter rule otherwise remain in force.
source_title: Airport Context Packet - MWAA (IAD and DCA)
supporting_excerpt: FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (enacted May 16, 2024) authorized 10 additional daily beyond-perimeter slot exemptions at DCA (5 nonstop round-trips). DOT awarded these in December 2024 to Alaska (SEA), American (SAN), Delta (SFO), Southwest (SAT), and United (LAS), with service starts staggered from February through March 2025.
caveat: Context packet is a Stage 0 secondary summary; underlying statutory text is P.L. 118-63 and DOT slot-award orders.

claim: MWAA maintains a mandatory seven-volume 2020 Design Manual plus Specifications and Estimating and Scheduling Standards issued by the Office of Engineering; the Manual is described by MWAA as having the force of law on airport property and is updated annually with airport-specific supporting volumes for IAD and DCA.
supporting_excerpt: MWAA maintains a seven-volume 2020 Design Manual, plus Specifications and Estimating and Scheduling Standards, issued by the MWAA Office of Engineering.
caveat: Whether the current Design Manual already contains binding acoustic, PA-zoning, STI, or LEQ requirements was not verified in this brief.

claim: MWAA plans approximately $5.5 billion of new debt between 2025 and 2028; adjusted debt per O&D enplanement is projected to peak near $400 in 2028; net revenue debt service coverage is expected to fall from 1.63x in 2024 to roughly 1.3x over the next five years.
source_title: Airport Context Packet - MWAA (IAD and DCA)
page_or_section: Section 3 - Financial position and debt capacity
supporting_excerpt: MWAA plans approximately $5.5 billion of new debt between 2025 and 2028. Adjusted debt per origin-and-destination enplanement is projected to peak near $400 in 2028... Net revenue debt service coverage is expected to fall from 1.63x in 2024 to roughly 1.3x over the next five years.
units: USD; USD per O&D enplanement; net revenue coverage ratio
caveat: Underlying primary sources are Fitch/Moody's/S&P rating reports (May 2025); confirm against those before quoting to a rating audience.

claim: IAD carried 29.01 million passengers in 2025, of which 10.53 million were international (roughly 36%+ international share, one of the highest among major U.S. airports); DCA carried 24.89 million passengers in 2025, down 5.4% year over year following the January 29, 2025 midair collision, federal shutdown, and softer government-related demand.
source_title: Airport Context Packet - MWAA (IAD and DCA)
page_or_section: Section 6 - Passenger and operational context (2025 calendar year)
supporting_excerpt: IAD: 29.01 million passengers, up 6.4% year-over-year; 10.53 million international passengers, roughly 36%+ international share... DCA: 24.89 million passengers, down 5.4% year-over-year.
caveat: Primary sources are MWAA traffic releases; the packet is a Stage 0 summary.

claim: Following the January 29, 2025 DCA midair collision, on March 14, 2025 the FAA removed the section of Helicopter Route 4 between Hains Point and the Woodrow Wilson Bridge from charts and restricted runways 15/33 and 4/22 during specific helicopter operations near DCA.
source_title: Airport Context Packet - MWAA (IAD and DCA)
supporting_excerpt: on March 14, 2025 the FAA removed the section of Helicopter Route 4 between Hains Point and the Woodrow Wilson Bridge from charts and restricted runways 15/33 and 4/22 during specific helicopter operations near DCA.
caveat: Underlying primary source is the FAA charting/NOTAM action; confirm against the FAA docket before quotation.

claim: The IAD $20 billion+ transformation was announced July 29, 2026 in a joint appearance by the President, the U.S. Transportation Secretary, United Airlines, and MWAA; program elements include more than 5 million square feet of new/refurbished facilities, replacement of Concourses C and D, extension of the AeroTrain, retirement of the mobile lounges, and preservation of the Saarinen Main Terminal.
source_title: Airport Context Packet - MWAA (IAD and DCA)
page_or_section: Section 5 - Capital program and named projects
supporting_excerpt: IAD '$20 billion+ transformation' was announced July 29, 2026 in a joint appearance by the President, the U.S. Transportation Secretary, United Airlines, and MWAA. Public descriptions include: More than 5 million ft² of new and refurbished facilities. Replacement of Concourses C and D. Extension of the AeroTrain and retirement of the mobile lounges. Preservation of the Eero Saarinen Main Terminal.
caveat: Program figure is a public-announcement top line, not a bond-financed number; scope will be documented in successor CIP filings.

claim: MWAA operates IAD and DCA under a long-term lease from the U.S. Department of Transportation; the 17-member Board of Directors has 7 members appointed by the Governor of Virginia, 4 by the Mayor of the District of Columbia, 3 by the Governor of Maryland, and 3 by the President of the United States, serving six-year terms with one reappointment permitted.
source_title: Airport Context Packet - MWAA (IAD and DCA)
supporting_excerpt: MWAA is governed by a 17-member Board of Directors with a split appointment: 7 members by the Governor of Virginia, 4 by the Mayor of the District of Columbia, 3 by the Governor of Maryland, and 3 by the President of the United States. Members serve six-year terms; one reappointment is permitted.
caveat: Presidential appointments create standing for federal actors beyond what most large-hub authorities carry; primary source is the Metropolitan Washington Airports Act and successor amendments.

claim: A new 15-year MWAA Airline Use and Lease Agreement took effect January 1, 2025, replacing the prior agreement, carrying at execution an approximately $9 billion capital construction program (approximately $6.99 billion at IAD and $2.39 billion at DCA).
source_title: Airport Context Packet - MWAA (IAD and DCA)
supporting_excerpt: A new 15-year Airline Use and Lease Agreement took effect January 1, 2025, replacing the prior agreement. At execution the agreement carried an approximately $9 billion capital construction program: approximately $6.99 billion at IAD (new 14-gate concourse, fifth-runway design work) and approximately $2.39 billion at DCA (restrooms and passenger amenities, eventual replacement of the Terminal 1 main concourse).
airport_or_entity: MWAA and signatory carriers at IAD and DCA
caveat: Majority-in-interest thresholds and cost-recovery categorization were not verified from primary documents in the context packet.

claim: ACRP Research Report 175, Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems, is the standing U.S. reference for PA intelligibility design guidance in passenger-processing environments.
source_title: ACRP Research Report 175: Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems (Transportation Research Board / Airport Cooperative Research Program)
source_citation: Transportation Research Board, Airport Cooperative Research Program, Research Report 175, 'Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems,' National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2017)
supporting_excerpt: ACRP Research Report 175 - Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems (Transportation Research Board / FAA-sponsored) is the standing U.S. reference for PA intelligibility design guidance for passenger-processing environments.
caveat: ACRP reports are guidance, not regulation. Airport-specific adoption is discretionary and typically routes through the airport authority's design manual.
